title: Largest Pick Divisible By Three
statement:
Pick any subset of the positive numbers in nums (not necessarily contiguous, possibly empty) so that the sum of the picked numbers is a multiple of 3.

Return the largest such sum. The empty pick has sum 0, so the answer is never negative.

examples.why: The total is 16, one too many. Dropping the 1 (the smallest number with remainder 1) leaves 15.
The total 44 has remainder 2. Dropping one 11 loses 11, but dropping both 1s (remainder 1 + 1 = 2) loses only 2.
5 is not a multiple of 3, so the best pick is the empty one.

hints: Only the remainder of each number mod 3 matters for divisibility. What does the best sum look like for each remainder?
Keep best[0], best[1], best[2]: the largest sum seen so far with each remainder. How does one new number update them?
For a number x, every old best[r] can either skip x or add it, moving to remainder (r + x) mod 3. Update from a copy of the old values. The answer is best[0].

explain.intuition:
Divisibility by 3 depends only on remainders, so you do not need to remember which numbers you picked, just the largest sum for each remainder 0, 1 and 2. That is three numbers of state, like a reducer that folds the array.

When a new number x arrives, each current best sum with remainder r may take x and become a candidate for remainder (r + x) mod 3. Keep whichever is larger, the old value or the new candidate. Read from a snapshot of the old values so that x is not used twice in the same step.
steps: Set best = [0, −∞, −∞]: only remainder 0 is reachable with the empty pick.
For each remainder r, set best[(r + x) % 3] = max(best[(r + x) % 3], old[r] + x).
pitfalls: Only ever dropping one number. When the total has remainder 2, dropping two numbers with remainder 1 can be cheaper, as in the second example.
Updating best in place while reading it, which may add the same number twice.
Starting best[1] and best[2] at 0. Then an impossible sum looks reachable.

solutions.title: Try every subset
solutions.idea: Enumerate all 2^n picks with a bitmask and keep the best sum divisible by 3.

solutions.title: Drop the cheapest remainder fix
solutions.idea: Take everything. If the total has remainder r, remove either the smallest number with remainder r or the two smallest with the other non-zero remainder.

solutions.title: DP over remainders
solutions.idea: Keep the largest sum for each remainder. Each number can be skipped or added to any of them.

followups: Generalise to divisibility by any k. What is the cost of the DP now?
Return the picked numbers, not just the sum.
